claims.text: Premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by thermodynamically driven surface segregation.
Au and Cu segregate toward the surface of heated AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Au and Cu are both lower-surface-energy and lower-melting-point constituents of the AuCoCuNiPt system.
Surface segregation of Au and Cu creates a thin, liquid-like surface layer.
The segregated surface layer begins melting significantly below the nanoparticle core.
The nanoparticle core remains crystalline until temperatures above the onset of surface premelting.
The thermodynamic drive to minimize total surface energy causes Au and Cu surface segregation.
Lower cohesive energies of the surface-enriched elements reduce the local melting point.
The initial nanoparticles have homogeneous elemental distributions at room temperature.
Reducing the fraction of low-surface-energy elements or kinetically suppressing their mobility will inhibit formation of the segregated surface layer.
Standard nanoparticles will show an onset of surface melting tens of kelvin earlier than modified-control nanoparticles.
Standard nanoparticles will show greater surface enrichment of low-surface-energy elements than modified-control nanoparticles during heating.
Controls with reduced low-surface-energy-element content or a more uniform elemental distribution will not exhibit the same early premelting behavior.
Melting of the modified controls will occur closer to the bulk melting temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equimolar multicomponent nanoparticles over the 3–10 nm and approximately 300–1000 K ranges.
The mechanism may not apply to substantially larger particles or simpler binary alloys.
Particle size, synthesis conditions, and kinetic factors may affect the premelting-temperature shift and premelted-layer thickness.
Failure to observe either an earlier premelting onset or greater surface enrichment in the standard particles would falsify the proposed segregation-driven mechanism.
